catalog_quote: The initial syllable is stressed if it is heavy, otherwise the second syllable is stressed. Any initial disyllabic foot necessarily takes the canonical form short unstressed + long stressed. An alternating length pattern, possibly indicating iterative iambic footing, is noted. (Hayes 1995:261, StressTyp2 passage 1457) ... Kroeber 1911:279: The stress accent of words does not tend so strongly as in some languages to rest on the penult, but may be found on any syllable between the first and the last. ... It seems that long vowels and vowels followed by a glottal stop or doubled consonant generally bear the accent, which is well marked.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.deciding_source_kind: database or survey citing another work
audit.deciding_source_year: 1995 (Hayes, carried in StressTyp2 2015 dump); primary 1951 (Freeland); corroboration 1911 (Kroeber)
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the carried Hayes 1995:261 text is verbatim in the held StressTyp2 SQL dump (passage 1457) and the Kroeber 1911:279 sentences are verbatim on the Rosetta page scan we hold/scanned; Hayes's own p.261 is not yet obtained. (2) The classification (weight-sensitive, left edge, CVV+CVC heavy, initial-if-heavy-else-second with lengthening) is exactly what the primary reference grammar says: Freeland 1951 secs.6-7 (pp.8 p.9 explicitly extending the prosodic description to the Northern dialect. So nothing suggests the classification is wrong; the 'contra' (9/16 Kroeber numerals) tests the rule against 1908-1911 pre-phonemic transcriptions with under-marked length and does not outweigh Freeland. (3) The record's grade is 'quotation carried over second-hand from StressTyp2' because the deciding quote is the StressTyp2 paraphrase; it can be upgraded by re-anchoring

sources.quote: One fixed major stress per word, on syllable 1 if it is long (CVV, CVC incl. C before another C / long C), otherwise on syllable 2, which is then long; secondary stress mostly word-final; LL disyllables have no major stress; stated for western Central dialect but explicitly generalized to Northern and Southern Sierra.
sources.locator: p.6 sec.6 (long syllable = long vowel, or short vowel + long consonant or two consonants); p.7 sec.7.1 Major stress ('always either the first or second syllable.. always long. If the first syllable of a word is long, it is always stressed.. if the first syllable is short it is never stressed, and the second syllable is long and stressed'); p.7-8 sec.7.2 secondary stress most frequently on the final syllable; p.8 sec.7.3 stressless LL disyllables; p.9 sec.8 prosody 'may.. be taken as applying to any of the Sierra dialects'
